title: NVIDIA unveils GR00T 2 world-action model and Isaac Lab 3.0 at CoRL
subtitle: The 2-billion-parameter transformer, built on Cosmos-Predict2.5, learns dexterous behaviors from human video and claims 40% zero-shot success on 50 held-out tasks.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: NVIDIA announced GR00T 2 at CoRL 2026 in Austin on November 9, alongside Isaac Lab 3.0 and a developer preview of Isaac Lab-Arena 0.4. GR00T 2 is a 2-billion-parameter transformer built on Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B and is pitched as an open frontier world action model — trained in part on human egocentric and third-person video rather than on robot teleoperation alone. NVIDIA reports 40% zero-shot success on 50 tasks absent from the target robot's training data, a benchmark that stresses the hardest problem in modern robot learning: generalizing to a body or a workspace the model has never seen. Isaac Lab 3.0 adds new photorealistic simulation assets, scalable domain randomization, and a reinforcement-learning path for dexterous hand manipulation, and the companion Isaac Lab-Arena preview standardizes benchmark suites so different robot platforms can be compared on the same tasks.

The design choice that matters is the shift to human video as the primary pretraining signal. Teleoperated robot data is expensive, scarce, and tied to specific hardware, which caps how well a model can generalize across embodiments. Human video is cheap, abundant, and already covers the full vocabulary of dexterous behavior — cooking, assembly, repair, caregiving — but the mapping from a human hand to a robot gripper is non-trivial, and prior work has mostly used human video as weak supervision rather than as the training backbone. GR00T 2 treats the world-action model as a single transformer that attends across modalities — Cosmos handles the physics-aware world model, and the action head is trained to output embodiment-conditional control. If the 40% zero-shot number holds up in third-party replication, it is a meaningful step toward the humanoid-generalist stack that Figure, 1X, Agility, and Unitree have been racing to build.

This lands at a loud moment in physical AI. Google DeepMind shipped Gemini Robotics 2 in July, Meta's physical-AI efforts have expanded, and Chinese labs — Unitree, XPeng, Nature Will — are releasing their own humanoid foundation models on an aggressive cadence. The commercial read is that NVIDIA wants Cosmos and Isaac to be the default substrate for humanoid foundation-model training the way CUDA is the default for LLM training. Openness is a question mark: NVIDIA calls GR00T 2 open, but the research page says code and weights will be released in December, and no license has been named publicly. Until weights ship, the 40% number is a claim, not a result that can be audited.

A takeaway for learners: in robotics, the bottleneck is almost never the model. It is the data — specifically, whether you can collect enough of the right kind without needing a warehouse full of robot arms and operators. The move toward training on human video is the most important shift in the field right now, and it is worth understanding why. Watch what happens when the weights drop, and try to read the eval section of the GR00T 2 paper rather than the launch post: the real story in a robotics release lives in which tasks the model fails, not which it passes.
